You cannot have resilience if every minute of your time is organized from the moment you arrive at school until after dinner. School days are long, homework piles up, and extracurricular activities fill the schedule, leaving no room for personal reflection or self-chill. This intentional lack of downtime destroys reflection and makes it impossible to learn anything meaningful.

So, this system is really bad because if you're a normal person from a non-rich family, going to Harvard actually sets you up for failure in life. First, it makes you arrogant; you think your knowledge trumps everyone else's and you stop asking questions or learning more. Second, utilitarianism takes over—your interests are limited to things that directly help you succeed. You lose the ability to explore and be creative.

If you come from a rich family, this system trains you for power, but if you're like me, you need to work hard, be talented, and be committed to your passion to succeed. This system breaks all that; it traumatizes people who had dreams of going to Ivy League schools only to fail in life due to lack of resilience, open-mindedness, and a commitment to learning beyond just success.

If you're rich, go to Harvard or Yale because you'll become richer. But if you're poor, attending these schools might be a mistake. For me, it was a failure; after graduation, I struggled with depression and spent years in my parents' basement playing video games, traumatized by the experience. To overcome this trauma, I had to relearn how to be open-minded, embrace failure, and develop resilience.

Psychologists have identified two modes of being: altruistic and utilitarian. Altruism is about connections and community, while utilitarianism is fight or flight. These mindsets are mutually exclusive; one cannot engage in both fully. The altruistic mindset fosters creativity but can be overwhelmed by the need for survival in emergencies.

In conclusion, the system at Harvard and Yale is designed to train future leaders, but it fails those from less privileged backgrounds. Success requires a blend of both modes—altruism and utilitarianism—but not at the cost of personal well-being and resilience.
